title: Clontarf's historic fishing sheds and Vernon Avenue
summary: Official historical material describes an early Clontarf fishing settlement with herring sheds fronting the Coast Road, and identifies Vernon Avenue as developing northward from the route by the sheds.
supported: Dublin City Council's 2026 Vernon Avenue preliminary design report supports the broad relationship between the herring-shed cluster, Coast Road and the avenue's origins. A specialist street-history article transcribes an 1836 Ordnance Survey Name Book description and discusses an earlier Green Lane name.
limits: The exact shed footprints and the precise route alignment have not been established. The 1836 wording and the 1816 Green Lane label remain secondary-source transcriptions until the original Name Book and Taylor map are inspected.

title: 1792 manuscript survey: Slip Field near Clontarf
summary: The National Library of Ireland catalogue records a 1792 survey by John Brownrigg, titled A survey of a piece of ground called the Slip field near Clontarf. Call number MS 21 F. 51 / (081), scale 10 perches to an inch.
supported: The manuscript map's title, date, surveyor, scale and catalogue identifier are recorded by the NLI. The catalogue says a digital copy exists.
limits: The image has not been visually inspected. 'Near Clontarf' does not establish that this field depicts the fishing sheds, Coast Road or Vernon Avenue. No map geometry or pin is inferred.

title: 1792 manuscript map: Bay View & Mount Pleasant
status_label: REGIONAL COMPARISON LEAD · IMAGE NOT INSPECTED
summary: A second John Brownrigg manuscript map in the NLI Longfield Map Collection is titled A map of Bay View & Mount Pleasant in the Barony of Coolock & County of Dublin belonging to Robert Burton Esq., dated 1792. Call number MS 21 F. 51 / (079).
supported: The NLI catalogue identifies the title, creator, date, collection and scale of 10 perches to an inch.
limits: Its precise geographic extent and relationship to the historic Clontarf sheds remain unknown until the image is inspected. It is not currently a confirmed sheds location.

title: Taylor's 1816 map and the reported Green Lane name
summary: Taylor's Map of the Environs of Dublin, Extending 10 to 14 Miles from the Castle, was published in 1816. UCD Library identifies the National Library of Scotland record, while the Vernon Avenue street-history article also cites the Virtual Treasury of Ireland catalogue item LBC-GJ-13-2 as an access route.
supported: The map's identity and date are supported by the catalogue and UCD Library guide. A secondary street-history article reports that the route was labelled Green Lane and cites the Virtual Treasury catalogue item LBC-GJ-13-2 for Taylor's map.
limits: The Clontarf portion of the 1816 map has not yet been visually inspected. The Green Lane label remains a secondary-source claim, not a direct reading of the original map. The Virtual Treasury page was reachable as a catalogue URL in this investigation, but its map image or Clontarf sheet was not extracted or inspected.

title: Rocque's Dublin maps: three dates, distinct works
summary: The 1756, 1757 and 1760 Rocque maps are distinct publications and should not be treated as interchangeable. The Vernon Avenue secondary article itself has a date/footnote mismatch, while Dublin City Council labels its reproduced map 1757.
supported: UCD Library and the Dictionary of Irish Biography distinguish several Rocque titles and dates. Dublin City Council's 2026 report labels its reproduced map 1757.
limits: The exact original sheet behind each modern reference has not yet been identified. No claim is made that a particular Rocque sheet proves the location of individual sheds.

title: The 1836 Ordnance Survey Name Book: primary entry still to inspect
summary: The NLI catalogue lists four typed-copy volumes of the County Dublin Ordnance Survey Name Books. Volume I, call number BB6442, covers Aderrig to Coolock and is the correct volume to investigate for Clontarf.
supported: The County Dublin collection is separate from the digitised City of Dublin compilation. The 1836 wording about a road through 'The Sheds of Clontarf Village' is currently known through a secondary article.
limits: The original County Name Book entry has not been directly inspected. The City of Dublin Name Book PDF is not a substitute for the County volume.

title: 1837: contemporary description of the Clontarf sheds
status_label: CONTEMPORARY PRINTED SOURCE · DIRECT TEXT INSPECTED
summary: Samuel Lewis's 1837 Topographical Dictionary describes wooden buildings along Clontarf's water edge, called the Clontarf sheds and formerly used to cure fish. It also records a profitable oyster bank off the sheds.
supported: The digitised 1837 parish entry explicitly links the Clontarf sheds to the coastal edge and fish curing. It places an oyster bank offshore from the sheds. This is strong contemporary printed evidence for the fishing-sheds locality and its maritime economy.
limits: The text does not give a surveyed boundary, the number or footprints of individual sheds, or an exact modern coordinate. 'Along the water's edge' must not be converted into a precise map polygon.

title: 1792: Patrick Toole's will abstract names the Sheds of Clontarf
status_label: PUBLISHED ARCHIVAL ABSTRACT · UNDERLYING RECORD NOT INSPECTED
summary: The Irish Manuscripts Commission's digitised Registry of Deeds Abstracts of Wills, Volume III, identifies Patrick Toole's property in the Sheds of Clontarf and a dwellinghouse in the Green of the Sheds. The entry is dated 11 September 1792, not 1789.
supported: The searchable published abstract identifies Patrick Toole, Sheds of Clontarf, County Dublin, and the date 11 September 1792. It refers to leasehold and other property in the Sheds and a dwellinghouse in the Green of the Sheds.
limits: The original memorial/deed has not been inspected directly. The abstract does not identify a precise plot, establish the physical location of the house, or map any shed footprints. Earlier project metadata incorrectly dated this entry 1789; that error is corrected in this update.

title: A reported 1728 map label: “Herring Sheds” at Clontarf
status_label: SECONDARY MAP TRANSCRIPTION · ORIGINAL IMAGE CHECK PENDING
summary: Dillon Cosgrave's local-history account states that Captain Perry's 1728 Map of Dublin Bay and Harbour marks “Herring Sheds” at the coast road below Vernon Avenue.
supported: The published chapter explicitly attributes the label to the 1728 map and places it at the Clontarf Sheds locality. The Dublin Port Archive catalogue independently identifies a 1728 map titled A New and Correct Map of the Bay and Harbour of Dublin with a small Plan of the City.
limits: The original map label and its exact position have not been independently read from the map image. Do not treat this secondary transcription as a georeferenced point or proof of exact shed geometry. The map's provenance and reproduction permissions must be respected.

title: 1785: a print titled The Sheds of Clontarfe
status_label: BRITISH LIBRARY PRINT IDENTIFIED · IMAGE INSPECTION PENDING
summary: The British Library's King's Topographical Collection inventory lists an 1785 print titled The Sheds of Clontarfe, by Thomas Malton after Francis Wheatley, shelfmark Maps K.Top.53.25. This is a direct visual-source lead specifically titled for the Clontarf sheds.
supported: The catalogue inventory gives the title, maker attribution, date and British Library shelfmark. A digitised dictionary of Irish artists also records Malton's 1785 aquatint after Wheatley.
limits: The print image has not yet been inspected at adequate resolution. We cannot yet describe buildings, shoreline, viewpoint or exact geography from its title alone. The higher-quality scan and reproduction terms need to be obtained from the British Library.

title: 1704: an early survey of the Parish of Clontarf
status_label: MANUSCRIPT MAP CATALOGUED · COVERAGE OF SHEDS UNCHECKED
summary: A 1704 survey by John Greene Junior is catalogued by the Virtual Treasury as a map of lands in the Barony of Coolock and Parish of Clontarf. Its stated boundaries include the Strand and Upper Hollybrook.
supported: The Virtual Treasury catalogue provides the map's date, creator, reference code DCLA C1 S1/130 and boundary description. This establishes a useful early cadastral source for the wider parish.
limits: The map image has not yet been inspected to establish whether it covers the Sheds or the relevant shoreline. Its title and parish-wide scope do not prove that the Sheds appear on the sheet. No map geometry or pin is inferred.

title: A possible earlier name: Herringtowne, 1693
status_label: SECONDARY HISTORICAL CLAIM · ORIGINAL CHART INSPECTION PENDING
summary: A Clontarf historical report states that the Sheds fishing-port was referred to as Herringtowne in Greenville Collins' 1693 map of the area.
supported: The secondary report explicitly attributes the name Herringtowne to Collins' 1693 map. This creates an earlier name-search lead for the fishing settlement.
limits: The original chart and exact label have not been inspected. Do not treat Herringtowne as a verified map transcription or assume that it labels precisely the same footprint later called the Sheds.

title: 1786: Christmas Weekes and water supply at Clontarf
status_label: HISTORICAL LETTER TRANSCRIPTION · ORIGINAL RECORD PENDING
summary: A published transcription reproduces a 30 November 1786 letter from Christmas Weekes at Clontarf thanking the County Grand Jury for recognition of works supplying shipping with water and other uses.
supported: The transcription identifies Weekes, Clontarf, the date and the subject of water-supply works. This may add an infrastructure strand to the story of the Sheds and the coastal settlement.
limits: The original Grand Jury record has not been inspected. The letter does not establish a precise pipe route, exact location of a water source or individual shed locations.
